questions.learningObjective: evaluate a circulation using Stokes and the curl
questions.stem: Along the unit circle in the plane z equal to 0, traversed once counterclockwise as seen from above, runs a field of F of x comma y comma z equal to minus y over 2, x over 2, 0. What is the integral of F dotted with the unit tangent around that closed path? Report the number only.

The direct route agrees: along the circle the field dotted with the unit tangent is one half at every point, and integrating a constant one half over a full turn of length 2 pi gives pi. A student who forgets the one half in the field reports 2 pi, and one who uses the divergence instead of the curl reports 0.
questions.hint: The curl of this field is a single constant vector, so the flux through the disk is just that constant times the disk's area.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: explain the content of Stokes and why it is useful
questions.stem: Explain what Stokes' theorem asserts, why the choice of spanning surface does not affect the answer, and what that freedom is good for.

answer.exemplar: Stokes' theorem asserts that the integral of a field around a closed curve equals the integral of its curl over any surface whose boundary is that curve, with the two orientations matched by the right-hand rule. The reason the surface can be chosen freely is that two surfaces with the same boundary differ by a closed surface lying between them, and the difference between the two curl fluxes is the flux of the curl through that closed surface, which vanishes when the field is smooth throughout the region between them. That freedom is the practical point: for a loop drawn as several straight edges, replacing four or five edge integrals by a single surface integral is a large saving, and one is free to choose a spanning surface that is flat, or a patch on a familiar surface, or otherwise easy to parameterise. The catch is that the curl must exist and be continuous everywhere on the chosen surface, so a spanning surface that passes through a singularity of the field is not available and must be rerouted.

questions.explanation: The exemplar has to give the reason the surface choice is free, since without it the freedom reads as an unjustified licence.
questions.hint: Compare two spanning surfaces: their difference is a closed surface, so ask what the theorem says about flux through a closed surface.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: explain the content of the divergence theorem and its local reading
questions.stem: Explain what the divergence theorem asserts, and explain why a zero total flux through a closed surface says the divergence vanishes inside without saying the field does.

answer.exemplar: The divergence theorem asserts that the total outward flux of a field through a closed surface equals the volume integral of its divergence over the region enclosed. Written pointwise, the divergence is the net rate of outflow per unit volume at a single point, so the theorem is the statement that the local accumulation rates add up to the net amount crossing the boundary. The second part follows immediately: a zero total flux forces the integral of the divergence to be zero, and applying the same reasoning to every sub-region inside forces the divergence to vanish pointwise. But the field itself is a different quantity. A field can have identically zero divergence while being large and non-zero, as the field of x, minus y, 0 shows on the unit cube, because divergence measures local spreading and not local size. Confusing the two is what leads people to expect a field to vanish wherever its total flux does.

questions.explanation: The exemplar has to separate the divergence from the field itself, since that separation is the whole point of the second question.
questions.hint: Read the divergence as a local rate, then ask what a zero integral of a local rate forces pointwise.

Green's theorem in its circulation form does this for a planar region, replacing a line integral around its boundary by the curl integrated over the area, which is the two-dimensional shadow of Stokes. Stokes does the same on a surface in three dimensions, and the divergence theorem does it for a solid, with a surface integral on the boundary and a volume integral inside. The operators differ because the interior is a different kind of object in each case, but the shape of the statement is identical.
questions.hint: Look for what each theorem equates: a boundary integral on one side, an interior integral on the other.

The downward orientation, since the thumb is drawn pointing away from the viewer and away is downward
options.misconception: reads a pictorial direction as though it were a coordinate direction

options.text: Neither, since the arrow lies outside the triangle and the rule only applies to an arrow drawn inside it
options.misconception: requires the arrow to be placed on the surface, which the rule does not

options.text: Both at once, since an anticlockwise boundary admits one normal from above and the opposite one from below

The catch is entirely in the word consistently: traversing the first arc from the shared start to the shared finish and then the second arc back from the finish to the start reproduces the original loop, whereas traversing both from start to finish produces two different open paths and a meaningless difference. Once the orientation is settled the combination is addition, and the same additivity is what lets a large loop be assembled from pieces that are individually easy.
questions.hint: Orient the two arcs so that together they trace the original loop once, then add.

The arc here is exactly half the circle and the integrand is constant along it, so the arc contributes half of pi, that is pi over 2, which is 1.5708. Stokes gives the same figure: the curl is 0 comma 0 comma 1, and its flux through the half disk it bounds is 1 times the area of a half disk of radius 1, which is pi over 2. questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: decide which of Stokes and the divergence theorem applies
questions.stem: Explain how to decide which of Stokes' theorem and the divergence theorem to reach for, given the shape of the object in front of you.

answer.exemplar: The deciding question is whether the object you have been handed is a boundary or an interior. If the given object is a closed curve, then Stokes applies and the useful move is to replace the circulation around it by a surface integral of the curl, choosing a spanning surface that is easy to parameterise rather than one that follows the curve. If the given object is a closed surface, then the divergence theorem applies and the move is to replace the total flux through it by a volume integral of the divergence over the solid it bounds, which is often far easier on a regular solid. If both a closed curve and a closed surface are present, the surface is usually the starting point, since the divergence theorem reduces it to a volume, and if a surface has a boundary the situation is a bit different again, with Stokes attaching the circulation around that boundary to the curl flux through it. The two theorems therefore meet on surfaces with boundaries, where the divergence theorem needs an added cap and Stokes gives a boundary circulation that must then be subtracted.

questions.explanation: The exemplar has to treat the case where a surface has a boundary, since that is where the two theorems actually interact.
questions.hint: Ask first whether you were handed a curve or a surface, and then whether it has a boundary.

questions.learningObjective: verify the divergence theorem on a cube face by face
questions.stem: Across the whole surface of the unit cube where each coordinate runs from 0 to 1, oriented outward everywhere, measure the field F of x comma y comma z equal to x, y, z. What is the total flux? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The divergence is the sum of three unit derivatives, which is 3 everywhere, and the cube has volume 1, so the divergence theorem makes the total flux 3. The face-by-face check is the instructive part because only half the faces contribute anything at all. On the face at x equal to 1 the outward normal is 1 comma 0 comma 0, so the flux is the integrand x, which is 1 everywhere on that face, giving 1. The same happens on the faces at y equal to 1 and z equal to 1, for three in total. On the three opposite faces the normal points along a negative coordinate while the corresponding component of the field is 0 there, so all three give 0. Summing gives 3, and the general lesson is that a position field only enters through whichever face its component points out of.
questions.hint: Only the faces where a component of the field points outward of the cube can contribute, and each contributes its constant value.

questions.learningObjective: read a table of divergences as a source profile
questions.stem: A one-dimensional profile is sampled along a line, and the divergence of a field takes the values -2, 1, 3, -1, 0 at five consecutive points. What can the record support?

options.text: There are regions of net outflow around the two positive samples and net inflow around the two negative ones

options.misconception: keeps one sample and discards the rest of a profile that is meant to be integrated

options.misconception: denies that a sampled profile is evidence about the field in a region

The sample of 0 marks a stretch in balance, which is a genuine and common situation and not a place where the field has vanished. questions.hint: Read the sign of each sample as outflow or inflow, and resist picking out only the largest one.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: interpret a moment of inertia physically
questions.stem: Two rigid bodies of the same total mass are compared, and one has all its mass concentrated close to an axis while the other has the same mass spread far from it. Which has the larger moment of inertia about that axis, and why?

options.text: The spread-out body, because the moment of inertia weights each piece by the square of its distance
The concentrated body, because mass nearer the axis resists a change of angle more strongly
options.misconception: assumes proximity to the axis increases the resistance to rotation

options.text: Both are equal, since the total mass is the same and distance plays no part in the calculation
options.misconception: ignores the distance weighting that defines a moment of inertia

options.text: Neither can be compared, since a moment of inertia depends on the axis chosen and no axis was specified
options.misconception: objects to the question when an axis was in fact given

questions.explanation: A moment of inertia integrates the square of the distance from the axis, so a piece of mass four times as far out counts sixteen times as much as the same piece near the axis. Spreading the same total mass outward therefore increases the moment of inertia, which is why a figure skater pulling in their arms spins faster and why a flywheel stores so much energy in its rim. The square is the crucial detail and the source of the strong effect: doubling every distance multiplies the moment of inertia by four rather than by two, and it is that convexity that makes the comparison so lopsided.
questions.hint: The integrand is the square of the distance, so compare the average squared distance rather than the average distance.

questions.stem: A surface is opened by removing a small patch, leaving a bowl rather than a closed shell. What goes wrong with computing a total flux through it?
